_readme: Raw survey records. VERBATIM LINES ARE THE SOURCE OF TRUTH — every figure in sources.csv is regenerated from these by scripts/build-dataset.mjs, so any disputed number traces to the line it came from and the factor that converted it. Do not edit the CSV by hand.
_caveat: Nothing here was read from a raw page. Every retrieval passed through a summarising layer that was independently caught fabricating a data point, corrupting arithmetic, and conflating two recipes. Treat quotations as needing re-verification.

_tiers.T1: page fetched, structured ingredient list returned
_tiers.T4: book transcription quoted by a third party

records.notes: The batter is meant to 'rise up and over the fruit as it bakes' — partial dispersion achieved by buoyancy rather than by mixing. This is the closest thing in the corpus to a fruit-dispersion mechanism.
quotes: cake topping is a light golden brown

records.title: Magic Cobbler

topping.verbatim: 1 stick butter melted in the pan

records.exclusionReason: Weakest source in the survey: folk canon, no named author, reconstructed from a search summary, no pan size. Recorded only to bound the batter-cobbler range.
flags: THE INVERSION IS REAL BUT ITS EXPLANATION IS NOT SOURCED. Butter goes in the pan, batter poured over unstirred, fruit on top unstirred; the layers change places during the bake. Every online account of the physics traces to content farms agreeing with each other and citing nothing.
records.notes: The inversion has a place-name-level trace: one etymology for 'sonker' is a dialect form of 'sinker', because the fruit sinks through the batter. That predates the internet by two centuries. The competing Scots etymology (sonker = grassy knoll) is at least as well supported — do not treat 'sinker' as settled.

records.title: Sonker, rolled pastry

topping.verbatim: 8 1/2 cups self-rising flour, for two pans
topping.inferredNote: halved to one pan; SR flour at a generic 125 g/cup — KA's own is ~113, an 11% error bar

flags: THE DRIEST TOPPING IN THE ENTIRE SURVEY at ~51 parts liquid per 100 flour — and it gets its rollability from VERY LOW FAT (14.5 vs a cobbler median of 45), not from low water. Combined liquid+fat is 65 against a cobbler median around 123.
This record is why the model's claim that rollable pastry lives at 22-35% hydration is wrong: the rolled-pastry sonker sits INSIDE the dough cluster.
fruit quantity NOT STATED — 'fruit filling of choice'
quotes: a close cousin to a cobbler, but juicier, more soupy

records.title: Sweet Potato Sonker with milk dip

topping.inferredNote: 6 oz by weight = 170 g; 3/4 cup by volume is ~181 g — a 6% ambiguity the source leaves open

fruit.inferredNote: sweet potato recorded under a fruit key for extraction purposes

flags: THE MILK DIP IS A DELIBERATE LATE-STAGE RE-WETTING — about 1/2 cup poured over at the 40-minute mark, then 15-20 minutes more. It is the exact inverse of steam venting, and any sog-resistance term inherited from the cobbler axis penalises this source for doing the thing it is trying to do.
records.notes: Rolled to 1/4 inch and VENTED for steam escape, with strips lining the dish sides. Calls its own dough a 'Sweet Biscuit Dough', not a pastry.
quotes: a juicy cobbler by any other name
Sonker features a biscuit crust rolled thin like pie dough, whereas cobblers typically use thicker drop-biscuit toppings

records.title: Vintage Appalachian Sonker, poured batter
flags: BATTER poured over HOT pre-baked fruit — the fruit is cooked 30 minutes first
records.notes: The richest sonker texture language in the corpus, and it explicitly rejects the crisp/crumble/biscuit target rather than approximating it.
quotes: Rather than a crunchy, crumbly top, or even a biscuity top, the batter is more like a pancake
it doesn't rise much, it's designed to stay flat
The fruit really steamed it like a dumpling, while the top baked to golden, buttery perfection
